Claude responded: Here's a paragraph you could use:

Here's a paragraph you could use:

Proficiency in Excel remains a foundational skill in business, even in an era increasingly shaped by artificial intelligence. While AI tools can automate analysis and generate insights at speed, they are most effective in the hands of someone who understands the underlying data and logic — and Excel builds exactly that understanding. Spreadsheets are the universal language of business: from financial modeling and budgeting to operations and marketing, nearly every professional role involves working with data in Excel at some level. Learning Excel also develops broader analytical habits — organizing information clearly, checking assumptions, and thinking systematically about problems — that transfer directly to working with AI tools and interpreting their outputs critically. In short, Excel is not made obsolete by AI; it is the foundation that makes AI more useful.

The core argument here is a two-part case: Excel has enduring practical value in the workplace, and it develops the analytical thinking needed to use AI well rather than blindly. That framing should resonate well with students who might otherwise wonder why they are learning a "manual" tool.

Claude responded: **Review: Introduction Chapter — Business Statistics by J.

Fetched: Business Statistics

Review: Introduction Chapter — Business Statistics by J. Alejandro Gelves

Overall Impression

This is a lean, purposeful introduction that gets out of the student's way quickly — a virtue in a course companion. It sets clear expectations, justifies its pedagogical choices, and strikes a warm but professional tone. For a practice-oriented workbook, the introduction does exactly what it should: orient, motivate, and invite.

Strengths

The opening epigraph from Epictetus is an inspired choice. It immediately frames the book's philosophy — that mastery comes from deliberate habit — without the author having to state it directly. It also signals that this is a thoughtful text, not just a technical manual.

The preface paragraph is well-crafted. The phrase "consistent, deliberate practice" echoes the Epictetan theme elegantly, and the acknowledgment of students is gracious and specific, which adds a human dimension that students will appreciate.

The "Excel in the era of AI?" section is the strongest piece of original writing in the chapter. The argument — that Excel builds the analytical foundation that makes AI more useful rather than being displaced by it — is coherent, well-reasoned, and genuinely reassuring to a student who might question the relevance of the course. The closing line is memorable and quotable.

Areas for Improvement

1. The "Why Excel?" section undersells itself. The bullet list of features (descriptive statistics, pivot tables, etc.) reads more like a product brochure than a compelling argument for why a student should invest time in this tool. Consider replacing or supplementing the list with one or two sentences about why these capabilities matter in a business context before listing them. The "Excel in the era of AI?" section actually makes a stronger case for Excel than "Why Excel?" does — consider reordering or merging these two sections.

2. A duplicated installation note. The "Installing Excel" section and the "How do I get Excel" section contain identical content and links. One should be removed. This small redundancy undermines the otherwise tight editing of the chapter.

3. The introduction is missing a roadmap. A brief overview of how the book is structured — what the chapters cover and in what sequence — would help students see the full arc of the course. Even two or three sentences pointing to the progression from descriptive statistics through inference and regression would orient readers and build anticipation.

4. The tone shift is slight but noticeable. The preface closes on a warm, almost lyrical note ("enjoy the journey"), but the subsequent sections feel more mechanical by comparison. A sentence or two of connective tissue — bridging the opening philosophy to the practical instructions — would smooth the transition.

Verdict

This is a confident and well-intentioned introduction that succeeds at its primary goals. With a few targeted revisions — particularly merging the Excel justification sections, removing the duplicate installation note, and adding a brief structural roadmap — it would be excellent. The writing is clear, the voice is consistent, and the pedagogical purpose is evident throughout. A solid foundation for what looks to be a practical and well-organized text.

markdown
## Frequency Distributions in Excel (Categorical)

To construct frequency distributions in Excel, we will use **pivot tables**. 
A pivot table is a powerful Excel tool that automatically summarizes and counts 
data, making it ideal for building frequency distributions. It allows you to 
quickly organize raw data into a structured table without writing any formulas.

**Example:** Let's use the food data to construct a frequency distribution. 
Download the data below and follow the steps to build the pivot table.

[{{< fa file-excel >}} Download Data](food_data.xlsx){.btn .btn-success}

**1. Select the Data:** Click on any cell within your data. Excel will 
automatically detect the range.

**2. Insert a Pivot Table:** Go to **Insert → PivotTable**. In the dialog box, 
confirm the data range and choose **New Worksheet** to place the pivot table 
in a new sheet. Click **OK**.

**3. Configure the Pivot Table:** In the PivotTable Fields panel on the right, 
drag the **Favorite Food** field to the **Rows** area and drag it again to the 
**Values** area. Excel will automatically count the occurrences of each food 
item, giving you the frequency distribution.

**4. Rename the Value Column:** By default, Excel labels the count column 
"Count of Favorite Food." You can double-click the header to rename it 
"Frequency" for clarity.

The video below walks you through each of these steps:

{{< video BarPlot.mov >}}

Once the pivot table is complete, you should obtain the following frequency 
distribution:

```{r echo=FALSE, message=FALSE, fig.align='center'}
library(ggthemes)
library(tidyverse)
library(gt)
food% rename(Food=value) %>% group_by(Food) %>% summarise(Frequency=n()) %>% 
  mutate(Relative=Frequency/sum(Frequency)) %>% gt() %>% 
  cols_align("center") %>% 
  tab_style(
    locations =cells_column_labels(columns = everything()),
    style = list(cell_borders(sides = "bottom", weight = px(3)),
                 cell_text(weight = "bold")))
```

Note that to obtain the relative frequency column in Excel, you can add a 
calculated column next to the frequency column. Simply divide each frequency 
by the total number of observations ($n=25$) using the formula `=B2/SUM($B$2:$B$5)`, 
where column B contains the frequencies. The `$` signs ensure the denominator 
remains fixed as you copy the formula down.

A few notes on the choices made:

  • The four-step structure mirrors how you handle the numerical frequency distribution steps later in the chapter, keeping the style consistent.
  • The relative frequency formula tip at the end bridges the pivot table output back to the concept introduced at the start of the section.
  • The video is placed after the written steps so students can read the instructions first and then watch the walkthrough — which tends to improve retention.

Claude responded: Pivot tables in Excel don't handle numerical bins as naturally as they do categorical data — but it is doable.

Pivot tables in Excel don't handle numerical bins as naturally as they do categorical data — but it is doable. Here are the two most common approaches:

Option 1: Add a helper column with bins (recommended for students)

This is the clearest approach for teaching purposes.

1. Create a Bin Column: In column C, add a header "Bin" and use the IFS formula to assign each stock price to a class:

excel
=IFS(B2<120,"[20,120)",B2<220,"[120,220)",B2<320,"[220,320)",B2<420,"[320,420)",B2<=520,"[420,520)")

Copy the formula down for all 30 rows.

2. Insert a Pivot Table: Go to Insert → PivotTable. Drag the Bin field to Rows and drag it again to Values to get the count.

3. Sort the Bins: Right-click any bin label in the pivot table → Sort → A to Z to get them in the correct order.

Option 2: Use the FREQUENCY function (no pivot table needed)

This is more compact but slightly more advanced:

1. Set up bin limits in a column (120, 220, 320, 420, 520).

2. Select an empty range of 5 cells next to your bins and enter:

excel
=FREQUENCY(B2:B31, D2:D6)

Then press Ctrl+Shift+Enter to confirm as an array formula.

My recommendation for the book is Option 1 — the helper column approach. It is more transparent, students can see exactly which bin each observation falls into, and it connects naturally to the pivot table workflow already introduced in the categorical section. Claude responded: Here's the section in your writing style:

Here's the section in your writing style:

markdown
## Frequency Distributions in Excel (Numerical)

To construct a frequency distribution for numerical data in Excel, we need 
an extra step compared to the categorical case. Since numerical data has no 
predefined categories, we must first create the bins manually using a helper 
column. Once the bins are in place, we can use a pivot table to count the 
observations in each class.

**Example:** Let's use the Dow Jones stock price data to construct a frequency 
distribution. Download the data below and follow the steps.

[{{< fa file-excel >}} Download Data](dow.xlsx){.btn .btn-success}

**1. Create a Bin Column:** In column C, add the header "Bin". In cell C2, 
enter the following `IFS` formula to assign each stock price to its 
corresponding class:

```
=IFS(B2<120,"[20,120)",B2<220,"[120,220)",B2<320,"[220,320)",
B2<420,"[320,420)",B2<=520,"[420,520)")
```

Copy the formula down for all 30 rows. Each stock price will now be assigned 
to one of the five classes defined in @sec-freqdistnum. Press `Ctrl + ~` to 
verify the formulas are correct, then press `Ctrl + ~` again to return to 
normal view.

**2. Insert a Pivot Table:** Click on any cell within your data. Go to 
**Insert → PivotTable**, confirm the data range, and select **New Worksheet**. 
Click **OK**.

**3. Configure the Pivot Table:** In the PivotTable Fields panel, drag the 
**Bin** field to the **Rows** area and drag it again to the **Values** area. 
Excel will count the number of stock prices in each bin, giving you the 
frequency distribution. You should obtain the following result:

| Bin | Frequency |
|-----------|-----------|
| [20,120)  | 9         |
| [120,220) | 12        |
| [220,320) | 5         |
| [320,420) | 3         |
| [420,520) | 1         |

**4. Insert a Histogram:** With the pivot table selected, go to 
**Insert → Charts → Clustered Column**. Excel will generate a bar chart. 
To convert it into a proper histogram, right-click on any bar and select 
**Format Data Series**. Set the **Gap Width** to **0%**. This removes the 
spaces between bars, which is the key visual distinction between a bar chart 
(used for categorical data) and a histogram (used for numerical data).

The video below walks you through each of these steps:

{{< video Histogram.mov >}}

A few notes:

  • The @sec-freqdistnum cross-reference links back to the numerical frequency distribution section where the five classes were derived, tying the Excel work back to the theory.
  • The Ctrl + ~ tip is included naturally within the steps rather than as a separate note.
  • I've used a placeholder Histogram.mov for the video — just replace it with whatever you name your recording.

Claude responded: The issue is that Excel sorts the bins alphabetically, so [120,220) comes before [20,120) because 1 comes before 2.

The issue is that Excel sorts the bins alphabetically, so [120,220) comes before [20,120) because 1 comes before 2. The fix is to add a number prefix to each bin label so Excel sorts them correctly:

excel
=IFS(B2<120,"1. [20,120)",B2<220,"2. [120,220)",B2<320,"3. [220,320)",
B2<420,"4. [320,420)",B2<=520,"5. [420,520)")

The pivot table will now sort as:

BinFrequency
1. [20,120)9
2. [120,220)12
3. [220,320)5
4. [320,420)3
5. [420,520)1

If you prefer to keep the bin labels clean without the number prefix, the alternative is to manually sort the rows in the pivot table by right-clicking on the [120,220) row → Move → Move Up until the order is correct. But the number prefix approach is simpler and more reliable, especially for students. Would you like me to update the section text to reflect this?

Claude responded: You're right — R makes it effortless.

You're right — R makes it effortless. In Excel the easiest native way is actually to use the Histogram chart type directly, which was introduced in Excel 2016. No pivot table, no helper column needed:

1. Select the stock price column (B1:B31 including the header).

2. Go to Insert → Charts → Statistical → Histogram. Excel automatically creates the bins and draws the histogram in one step.

3. Adjust the bins: Double-click the horizontal axis to open the Format Axis panel. You can set:

  • Bin width to 100
  • Underflow bin to 20

That's it — three steps versus the pivot table approach.

The tradeoff worth mentioning in your book:

The direct histogram approach is faster but gives students less control and less visibility into how the bins are constructed. The pivot table approach is more work but is more transparent — students can see exactly which bin each observation falls into, which reinforces the concepts from the theory section.

A reasonable recommendation for your book would be to teach the pivot table approach first so students understand the mechanics, and then mention the direct histogram as a shortcut once the concept is solid. Something like:

Now that you understand how bins are constructed, Excel also offers a faster route via Insert → Statistical → Histogram, which automates the binning process.

Would you like me to incorporate this into the section?

Claude responded: That's the key weakness of the direct histogram approach — you don't easily get the frequency distribution table.

That's the key weakness of the direct histogram approach — you don't easily get the frequency distribution table. The direct histogram just draws the chart without showing you the counts in a table. You would have to manually hover over each bar to read the frequency, which is not practical.

So the pivot table approach is actually better for teaching because it gives students both:

  1. The frequency distribution table — clearly showing the counts for each bin
  2. The histogram chart — built from the pivot table

The direct histogram shortcut is fine for a quick visual but doesn't support the full learning objective of constructing and interpreting a frequency distribution table.

I would suggest framing it this way in the book:

While Excel offers a direct histogram chart via Insert → Statistical → Histogram, this approach only produces the visual and does not generate a frequency distribution table. For that reason, we will use the pivot table approach, which gives us both the table and the chart in a transparent and reproducible way.

This also subtly reinforces the broader lesson that understanding the underlying process matters — which ties nicely back to the book's philosophy of deliberate practice. Shall I update the full section with this note included?

Claude responded: The issue is that your section label {#freqdistnum} is on the Frequency Distributions (Numerical) heading, but the reference @sec-freqdistnum requires the sec-…

The issue is that your section label {#freqdistnum} is on the Frequency Distributions (Numerical) heading, but the reference @sec-freqdistnum requires the sec- prefix to be part of the label itself. Change the label on your heading from:

markdown
## Frequency Distributions (Numerical) {#freqdistnum}

to:

## Frequency Distributions (Numerical) {#sec-freqdistnum}

That's it — Quarto's cross-reference system requires the sec- prefix to be in the label, not just in the @ reference. Once you make that change, @sec-freqdistnum in the Excel section will render as a clickable hyperlink like "Section 2.1" or whatever numbering your book assigns to it.

Claude responded: To indent the answer content to align with the question text, wrap the content inside the <details> block with a <div> that has left padding:

To indent the answer content to align with the question text, wrap the content inside the <details> block with a <div> that has left padding:

markdown
### Exercise 1 {.unnumbered}
You will need the **Brain Cancer** data set to answer this question. You can get the data using the link below:

[{{< fa file-excel >}} Download Data](dow.xlsx){.btn .btn-success}

1.  Construct a frequency and relative frequency table of the *Diagnosis* variable. What was the most common diagnosis? What percentage of the sample had this diagnosis?

<details>
<summary>Answer</summary>
<div style="padding-left: 1.5em;">

*The most common diagnosis is Meningioma, a slow-growing tumor that forms from the membranous layers surrounding the brain and spinal cord. The diagnosis represents about* $48.28$% of the sample.

*The frequency distribution should have the following numbers:*

```{r echo=FALSE, message=FALSE}
library(ISLR2)
table(BrainCancer$diagnosis)
```

*The relative frequency distribution has the following numbers:*

```{r echo=FALSE, message=FALSE}
freq<-table(BrainCancer$diagnosis)
prop.table(freq)
```

</div>
</details>

The key change is adding <div style="padding-left: 1.5em;"> right after <summary>Answer</summary> and closing it with </div> before </details>. You can adjust 1.5em to 2em or 3em if you want more indentation. Note the blank lines inside the <div> are important — Quarto needs them to correctly render the R code chunks and markdown inside HTML blocks.

Claude responded: Here's the updated _quarto.

Here's the updated _quarto.yml and a custom CSS file to give your book that editorial look — warm off-white background, strong serif headings, clean sans-serif body text, and bold typographic contrast inspired by the post:

In your _quarto.yml, update the format section:

yaml
format:
  html:
    theme: [cosmo, custom.scss]
    include-in-header: custom-head.html

Then create a new file called custom.scss in your project folder:

scss
/*-- scss:defaults --*/

// Fonts
$font-family-sans-serif: "Inter", sans-serif;
$headings-font-family: "Playfair Display", serif;

// Colors
$body-bg: #F5F0EB;
$body-color: #1a1a1a;
$link-color: #C0392B;

/*-- scss:rules --*/

// Import Google Fonts
@import url('https://fonts.googleapis.com/css2?family=Playfair+Display:wght@700;900&family=Inter:wght@400;500&display=swap');

// Headings
h1, h2, h3 {
  font-family: "Playfair Display", serif;
  font-weight: 900;
  color: #1a1a1a;
  letter-spacing: -0.5px;
}

h1 {
  font-size: 2.6rem;
}

h2 {
  font-size: 1.9rem;
  border-bottom: 3px solid #C0392B;
  padding-bottom: 6px;
  margin-top: 2rem;
}

// Body text
body {
  font-family: "Inter", sans-serif;
  font-size: 1rem;
  line-height: 1.8;
  background-color: #F5F0EB;
  color: #1a1a1a;
}

// Sidebar
.sidebar {
  background-color: #EDEAE5;
  border-right: 2px solid #C0392B;
}

// Code blocks
pre {
  background-color: #EDEAE5;
  border-left: 4px solid #C0392B;
  border-radius: 4px;
  padding: 12px;
}

// Details/Answer boxes
details {
  background-color: #EDEAE5;
  padding: 10px 16px;
  border: 1px solid #ccc;
  border-left: 4px solid #C0392B;
  border-radius: 4px;
  margin: 14px 0;
}

details summary {
  cursor: pointer;
  font-weight: 600;
  font-family: "Inter", sans-serif;
}

// Download button
.btn-success {
  background-color: #C0392B !important;
  border-color: #C0392B !important;
  color: white !important;
  font-family: "Inter", sans-serif;
  font-weight: 500;
}

.btn-success:hover {
  background-color: #1a1a1a !important;
  border-color: #1a1a1a !important;
}

// Page footer
.nav-footer {
  border-top: 2px solid #C0392B;
  font-size: 0.85rem;
  color: #555;
}

The key design choices that mirror the post's aesthetic:

  • Playfair Display for headings gives the strong editorial serif feel
  • Inter for body text keeps it clean and modern
  • Warm off-white (#F5F0EB) replaces the default white background
  • Deep red (#C0392B) as the accent color, used on borders, links, and buttons — echoing the red in the post
  • The h2 red underline gives chapter sections a strong visual anchor without being heavy-handed

7:07 PM

Claude responded: The simplest way is directly in RStudio:

The simplest way is directly in RStudio:

File → New File → Text File

Then when you save it (Cmd + S), name it custom.scss and make sure to save it in the same folder as your _quarto.yml file. That's it.

Alternatively you can do it from the Terminal tab in RStudio:

bash
touch custom.scss

This creates an empty custom.scss file in your project folder, which you can then open and paste the CSS into.

The Terminal approach is slightly faster if you're comfortable with it. Either way, the key is that custom.scss lives in the same directory as _quarto.yml.

Here are a few options you could use in Quarto. The cleanest approach is to use a custom callout block. Add this to your custom.scss:

// Example callout box

  background-color: #EDE8E3;
  border-left: 4px solid #C9856A;

  padding: 12px 16px;

  font-weight: 700;
  color: #C9856A;
  font-size: 1rem;
  margin-bottom: 6px;
}

Then in your .qmd file you would use it like this:

markdown
::: {.callout-note appearance="simple" icon=false}
**Example:** Consider a retail store analyzing its sales performance...
:::

However the simplest option that requires no scss changes is Quarto's built-in callout blocks. You have four styles to choose from:

markdown
::: callout-note
**Example:** Your example text here.
:::

::: callout-tip
**Example:** Your example text here.
:::

::: callout-important
**Example:** Your example text here.
:::

::: callout-warning
**Example:** Your example text here.
:::

My recommendation for your book is to use ::: callout-tip since it renders with a warm green tone that complements the terracotta palette nicely, or we can override its color in the scss to match terracotta exactly. Would you like me to do that?

**4. Add the Relative Frequency:** Next to the frequency column in the 
pivot table, add a new column labeled "Relative Frequency". In the first 
cell, enter the formula `=B2/SUM($B$2:$B$5)`, where column B contains 
the frequencies. The `$` signs lock the denominator so it does not change 
as you copy the formula down. Copy the formula down for all food items. 
Each value represents the proportion of students who selected that food 
item out of the total of 25.

The $ explanation is worth keeping — students often get tripped up by absolute versus relative cell references, and this is a natural place to introduce that distinction. Would you like me to add a similar step 4 to the numerical frequency distribution section as well?

markdown
**1. Create a Bin Column:** In column C, add the header "Bins". In cell C2, 
enter the following `IFS` formula to assign each stock price to its 
corresponding class:

```
=IFS(B2<120,"1. [20,120)",B2<220,"2. [120,220)",B2<320,"3. [220,320)",
B2<420,"4. [320,420)",B2<=520,"5. [420,520)")
```

Copy the formula down for all 30 rows. Each stock price will now be assigned 
to one of the five classes defined in @sec-freqdistnum. Press `Ctrl + ~` to 
verify the formulas are correct, then press `Ctrl + ~` again to return to 
normal view.

**2. Insert a Pivot Table:** Select the data. Go to `Insert → PivotTable`, 
confirm the data range, and select `Existing Worksheet`. Click `OK`.

**3. Configure the Pivot Table:** In the PivotTable Fields panel, drag the 
`Bins` field to the `Rows` area and drag it again to the `Values` area. 
Excel will count the number of stock prices in each bin, giving you the 
frequency distribution.

**4. Add the Cumulative Distribution:** Drag the `Bins` field to the `Values` 
area a second time. Click on the field in the `Values` area and select 
`Value Field Settings`. Click on the `Show Values As` tab and choose 
`% Running Total In` from the dropdown menu. Make sure the base field is 
set to `Bins`. Click `OK`. Excel will display the cumulative percentage for 
each bin, showing the proportion of stock prices that fall at or below each 
class. You should obtain the following frequency distribution:

| Bin           | Frequency | Cumulative % |
|---------------|-----------|--------------|
| 1. [20,120)   | 9         | 30.00%       |
| 2. [120,220)  | 12        | 70.00%       |
| 3. [220,320)  | 5         | 86.67%       |
| 4. [320,420)  | 3         | 96.67%       |
| 5. [420,520)  | 1         | 100.00%      |

**5. Insert a Histogram:** With the pivot table selected, go to 
`Insert → Charts → Clustered Column`. Excel will generate a bar chart. 
To convert it into a proper histogram, right-click on any bar and select 
`Format Data Series`. Set the `Gap Width` to `0%`. This removes the spaces 
between bars, which is the key visual distinction between a bar chart 
(used for categorical data) and a histogram (used for numerical data).

The video below walks you through each of these steps:
